blocks.text: Daniel slammed the laboratory door hard enough to rattle the windows. He set the surviving energy case on his bench and stared at its fading glow. Zerdo had smashed his machine. Billy and that reporter had watched him do it.
Luke hovered near the ceiling. “The fish got away.”
Daniel looked up. A living fish, shining with the very energy his robot needed. He had been collecting scraps when he could have taken the source.

He dragged a huge fishing net out of a storage cupboard and spread it across the floor. Lead weights lined its edges. He tied a small glass lamp in the middle and connected it to the last of the collected power.
Blue light filled the mesh.
“You’re going back tonight,” he told Luke. “No glove. No Zerdo. Just the fish.”
Luke eyed the net. His jaw still ached from striking the stone wall that afternoon.
“And then you fix me?”
“Once the robot works, nobody will stop us. Bring me that fish.”

Late that night, the streets beside the lake were quiet. Beyond them, Terminal Tower rose over Public Square. Seth had gone home after arranging to meet Billy and Jenny in the morning. Fist had stayed at Billy’s office, helping watch for Luke. Perch had promised to keep well away from the wrecked intake.
The blue lamp dropped into the water far beyond it.
Perch spotted the glow from below. For a moment he wondered if it came from whatever had landed in the lake. He swam closer, keeping beneath the rocks until he could see it clearly.
There was mesh behind the light.
He turned—but the weighted edges were already sinking around him. Above the surface, Luke pulled the ropes together with his iron jaws. Perch darted for the last opening. It closed against his fins.

Luke rose out of the darkness with the gathered net clenched between his teeth. Water streamed from it. Inside, Perch battered the mesh, furious and frightened, while the shoreline dwindled behind him.
blocks.alt: Jaws O’ Death flies above Lake Erie carrying the trapped Super Perch in a large fishing net held by his iron jaws.

blocks.text: Out of the lake, Perch could no longer use his swimming speed to escape. Every kick tangled him farther. He tried calling for Seth, but there was nobody below except empty streets.
Daniel was waiting with a tank of water on a wheeled stand. He tipped Perch into it, pulled the net clear, and locked its thick glass lid. Perch struck the wall hard enough to make the stand shudder.
“Look at you,” Daniel murmured. He could see the fish’s anger, but he could not understand its demands to be released.
He hoisted the tank into a cradle inside the robot’s chest, where a heart would have been. Cables ran from metal bands around the glass to the machine’s power terminals. He switched them on.
Perch’s blue glow spread along the cables. The robot straightened against its braces.

Both metal hands opened. A heavy foot lifted from its test cradle and came down with a boom that shook dust from the rafters. In the tank near its heart, Perch circled angrily as his energy fed the machine.
blocks.alt: The trapped Super Perch powers the robot from a water tank inside its chest while a small fiery watcher looks through the laboratory window.

blocks.text: Daniel laughed. He released one restraint, then another. This time the robot stayed upright.
“Tomorrow,” he said, “the city belongs to me.”
Luke hovered beside the workbench. His jaw still ached where it had struck the stone wall. “Now that it works, when can you put me back?”
Daniel adjusted a dial without looking at him. “After I know it’ll do what I need. The robot comes first tonight.”
Luke watched the needle settle. First the glove. Then enough power. Then the fish. He had brought the fish, and the machine was standing. His uncle was still looking past him.
He drifted toward the doorway but lingered there a moment. Behind him, Daniel reached for the controls.

High outside the workshop window, a small, round face hovered inside a crown of orange and yellow flames. Its large eyes narrowed at the tank. The fiery watcher had no body. He had followed the fish’s familiar power here, and what he saw made his flames flare. Daniel never looked up.
